title: Money and paperwork
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: L1-M8 TAUGHT quantī cōnstat AS A WHOLE PHRASE AND THIS MODULE CAN FINALLY EXPLAIN IT. quantī is a GENITIVE OF PRICE — 'at how much?' — and the genitive has now done three jobs: possession between people (L2-M2), the thing felt about (M6), and price. That is the third and last job L3 gives it. A learner who has been saying quantī cōnstat for two levels without knowing why is owed the reason at the moment the course can give it.

librī IS 'OF THE BOOK' AND ALSO 'BOOKS', SPELLED IDENTICALLY. The genitive singular and the nominative plural fall together in this whole class of noun and there is no mark for it — the sentence decides, and pretium librī can only be a price of one thing. L2-M2 met exactly this with magistrī and rebuilt a hero sentence around it rather than ship a note that would read wrong.

THE MONEY WORDS ARE CLASSICAL AND THE OFFICE WORD IS NOT, AND THE MODULE SAYS WHICH IS WHICH. pretium, solvō, mercēs and L1-M8's nummus are all Cicero's — Rome had contracts, rents, receipts and clerks, so mercēdem solvō and chartam signō are real. An office with a queue in it is not: officīna is a workshop put to a modern use by the living-Latin community and the Vatican's lexicon, the same named source L2-M7's tēlephōnum came from, and NOTHING IS COINED HERE. solvō is 'I loosen' — you pay a debt by untying it, which is the picture English keeps in 'settle' and 'discharge'.

charta IS A GREEK LOAN WITH A PLAIN a AND NO GREEK LETTERS IN IT. docs/123 §8 banned ȳ outright, because #631 measured it as undrawn by every bundled face — so a Greek-looking word in this course takes a plain vowel or is not used at all. Nothing in the build would catch a character the font cannot draw, which makes this an author's responsibility rather than a gate's.

ut PLUS A SUBJUNCTIVE IS STILL THE PURPOSE CLAUSE, FOUR MODULES ON: ad officīnam eō ut chartam signem. The plate is the plain present after ut, for the second time in the level, because a longer sentence is where a learner stops watching the mood. And a form in -am or -em may be a future or a subjunctive, which M4 named and S09 demonstrates: sī pretium magnum sit, nōn solvam — only sī and sit tell you solvam is imagined.

possum CLOSES L2-M8's GAP IN A SENTENCE ABOUT MONEY: nōn tamen solvere possum. That module said nōn inveniō and meant 'I cannot find' because no level below L3 had the verb. And nōn belongs to whichever word it stands in front of — nōn solvere possum would be 'I am able NOT to pay', which is a very different position from being unable to.

A NEUTER NOUN HIDES THE ACCUSATIVE OF REPORTED SPEECH. dīcit pretium magnum esse is M5's construction with nothing visibly moved, because pretium and magnum are neuter and their accusative is identical to their nominative. A learner who checks whether a sentence 'looks reported' will get this wrong in both directions — the construction is decided by the verb in front, never by the endings.

THE LAST SENTENCE OF THIS MODULE INTRODUCES NOTHING, ON PURPOSE. Quantī cōnstat? Melius est nōn emere — L1-M8's phrase and M7's advice frame, twenty-eight rungs apart and both in the learner's hands. A module this late should be able to end on a sentence that is entirely ladder.

sentences.cue: How much does the book cost?

words.note: 'At how much?' — a GENITIVE of price, which L1-M8 taught as a whole phrase and could not explain. Now it can: quantī cōnstat is 'at how much does it stand?'
'Book' as the subject — the thing that stands at a price. L1-M4's word.
'It costs', literally 'it stands together'. L1-M8's word, and English 'constant' is the same verb: a price is what a thing stands at.

sentences.trap: L1-M8 taught this as a phrase you said without knowing why, and here is the why: quantī is a GENITIVE of price, 'at how much'. The genitive now has three jobs — possession (L2-M2), the thing felt about (M6), and price — and L3 opens no fourth.
sentences.sound: QUAN-tī LI-ber CŌN-stat. The long ī of quantī is the case ending, and it is the whole of 'at how much'.

variations.changed: a different thing priced

variations.changed: more than one, so the verb goes plural

sentences.mnemonic: quantī is a price, not a question word.

sentences.cue: The price of the book is high.

words.note: 'Price', and it is neuter: pretium as the subject and as the object both. English 'precious' and 'appreciate' come from it.
'Of the book' — the GENITIVE, and it is L2-M2's possession job. It is also the shape L1-M1 taught as the PLURAL, 'books', which is the collision this note exists to name.
'Big', and of a price it means high. L2-M3's adjective in the neuter, agreeing with pretium.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.

sentences.trap: librī is 'of the book' here and 'books' in L1-M1, and the two are spelled identically. Latin has a small number of these and no mark for them — the sentence decides, and pretium librī can only be a price of one thing. L2-M2 met the same problem with magistrī and rebuilt a sentence around it.

variations.cue: The price of the table is high.
variations.changed: a feminine noun, whose genitive is mēnsae

variations.cue: The price of the book is not high.
variations.changed: the negative

variations.cue: The price is high.
variations.changed: nothing owned, so no genitive

mistake.why: the masculine ending, pulled by librī standing next to it. magnum agrees with pretium, which is neuter — and the word nearest an adjective is very often not the word it answers to, which is the error L2-M3 and L3-M2 both spent plates on.

sentences.mnemonic: Genitives and plurals can look alike.

words.note: 'Rent, wages' — mercēs as the subject, mercēdem as the thing paid. It is what is owed either way, whether you collect it or hand it over.
'I pay', and literally 'I loosen' — you pay a debt by untying it. solvō 'I pay', solvit 'he pays'. English 'solve' and 'dissolve' are the same word.

sentences.trap: solvō is 'I loosen' and paying is untying a debt, which is the same picture English keeps in 'settle' and 'discharge'. Every word in this module is classical — Rome had contracts, rents and receipts — and the metaphor is a Roman one rather than a translation.

variations.cue: I am not paying the rent.
variations.changed: the negative

variations.cue: He is paying the rent.
variations.changed: someone else paying

variations.cue: I can pay the rent.
variations.changed: M2's possum with the infinitive

words.note: 'Paper, a form' — a Greek loan, and it takes a plain a with no accent and no ȳ anywhere in it. English 'chart' and 'card' both come from it.
'I mark, I sign' — signō 'I sign', signat 'he signs', signāre 'to sign'. English 'sign' and 'signature' are the same word, and a Roman signed with a seal rather than a name.

sentences.trap: charta is a Greek loan and it is spelled with a plain a. docs/123 banned ȳ outright because no bundled face draws it, so a Greek-looking word in this course takes a plain vowel or is not used — and nothing in the build would catch a character the font cannot draw.

variations.cue: I am not signing the form.
variations.changed: the negative

variations.cue: I do not want to sign the form.
variations.changed: L1-M3's refusal with an infinitive

variations.cue: The form is here.
variations.changed: the noun as a subject, so the ending goes back

sentences.mnemonic: charta: a plain a, and no Greek letters.

sentences.display: Ad officīnam eō ut chartam signem.
sentences.cue: I am going to the office in order to sign the form.
sentences.literal: to office I-go so-that paper I-may-sign

words.note: 'To', with the object shape after it. L1-M4's preposition.
'Office, workshop' — a MODERN use of a classical word, from the living-Latin community and the Vatican's lexicon, the same named source M7's tēlephōnum came from. Nothing here is coined.
'I go': eō, īs, it, īmus, īre.
'So that' — with a subjunctive, and the purpose reading only. M4's word.
'That I may sign' — signō's present subjunctive. M4's mood, doing M4's purpose job.

sentences.trap: A Roman had contracts and clerks and had no office with a queue in it. officīna is a workshop put to a modern use by people who speak Latin now, and the module says so rather than pretending — the same honesty L2-M7 needed for the telephone and M9 will need for a festival.
sentences.sound: ad of-fi-CĪ-nam E-ō ut CHAR-tam SIG-nem. The long ī of officīnam is the stress, and the ch of chartam is a plain k.

variations.display: Ad officīnam eō ut mercēdem solvam.
variations.cue: I am going to the office to pay the rent.
variations.changed: a different purpose

variations.display: Ad officīnam it ut chartam signet.
variations.cue: He is going to the office to sign the form.
variations.changed: someone else, so both verbs move

variations.cue: I am going to the office.
variations.changed: no purpose clause, so no mood

mistake.display: Ad officīnam eō ut chartam signō.
mistake.why: the plain present after ut. A purpose clause is always subjunctive because a purpose is not a fact yet — M4's rule, and the plate is here again because a longer sentence is where it happens.

sentences.mnemonic: ut wants a mood, four modules on.

sentences.display: Pretium magnum est; nōn tamen solvere possum.
sentences.cue: The price is high; I cannot pay it, though.
sentences.literal: price big is not however to-pay I-can

words.note: 'Price', and it is neuter: pretium as the subject and as the object both. English 'precious' and 'appreciate' come from it.
'Big', and of a price high. L2-M3's adjective in the neuter.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.
'Not', and it denies possum rather than solvere. What is impossible is the paying.
'However', and it comes SECOND in its clause. M3's word.
'To pay' — solvō's infinitive, and the shape possum needs.
'I can': possum, potes, potest. M2's verb.

sentences.trap: L2-M8 said nōn inveniō and meant 'I cannot find', because no level below this one had possum. Here the real thing pays that off — and nōn belongs to possum, not to solvere: nōn solvere possum would be 'I am able not to pay', which is a very different position to be in.

variations.display: Pretium magnum est; solvere tamen possum.
variations.cue: The price is high; I can pay it, though.
variations.changed: the ability affirmed, with tamen still second

variations.display: Mercēs magna est; nōn tamen solvere possum.
variations.cue: The rent is high; I cannot pay it, though.
variations.changed: a feminine noun, so the adjective moves

variations.cue: The price is high; I am not paying.
variations.changed: a refusal instead of an inability

sentences.usage: Said turning something down on price.
sentences.mnemonic: nōn belongs to the word in front of it.

words.note: 'At how much?' — a GENITIVE of price, which L1-M8 taught as a whole phrase and could not explain. Now it can: quantī cōnstat is 'at how much does it stand?'
'Rent, wages' as the SUBJECT — mercēdem is the shape you pay. It is the same word either way, whether you collect it or hand it over.
'It costs', literally 'it stands together'. L1-M8's word.

sentences.trap: S03 wrote mercēdem and this writes mercēs, and the difference is what the word is doing: paying it makes it an object and asking its price makes it a subject. L1-M8's phrase works on anything, and this is the first module that can say why.

variations.cue: How much is it?
variations.changed: nothing named, which is the whole phrase L1-M8 taught

variations.cue: The rent is high.
variations.changed: an answer with an adjective instead

variations.cue: How much does the paper cost?
variations.changed: a different thing priced

sentences.usage: Said before you agree to anything.

sentences.cue: He says the price is high.

words.note: 'He says' — dīcō, dīcit, dīxit. M5's verb.
'Price' — neuter, so it looks the same as a subject and inside a reported clause. This is the one place the accusative of reported speech is invisible.
'Big', and of a price high. Neuter, agreeing with pretium — and it too looks unchanged.
'To be' — sum's infinitive. M3 opened it.

sentences.trap: Nothing moved, and the construction is still there. pretium and magnum are neuter, so their accusative is identical to their nominative — which means this is M5's reported clause with no visible sign of it. A learner who checks whether a sentence 'looks reported' will get this one wrong in both directions.

variations.cue: He says the rent is high.
variations.changed: a feminine noun, where both words DO move

variations.cue: He says he is paying the price.
variations.changed: M5's reflexive, and an object inside the clause

variations.cue: The price is high.
variations.changed: asserted rather than reported — and it looks identical

sentences.usage: Said passing on what a seller told you.

sentences.display: Sī pretium magnum sit, nōn solvam.
sentences.cue: If the price were high, I should not pay.
sentences.literal: if price big it-may-be not I-may-pay

words.note: 'If', and with the subjunctive it imagines rather than claims. M4's word.
'Price', and it is neuter: pretium as the subject and as the object both. English 'precious' and 'appreciate' come from it.
'Big', and of a price high. Neuter, agreeing with pretium.
'That it may be' — sum's present subjunctive in the it-shape. M4's mood.
'Not', in front of what it denies.
'That I may pay' — solvō's present subjunctive, and ALSO what its future would look like. M4 named that ambiguity and here it is in a real sentence: only sī and sit tell you which.

sentences.trap: solvam is the mood here, and it is also exactly what solvō's future would be. M4 said a form ending in -am may be either and that only the construction decides — and this sentence is the proof: sī plus sit makes the whole thing imagined, so solvam is imagined too.
sentences.sound: SĪ PRE-ti-um MAG-num SIT, nōn SOL-vam. The long ī of sī is the only length until the end.

variations.display: Sī pretium magnum sit, nōn emam.
variations.cue: If the price were high, I should not buy.
variations.changed: L1-M8's verb in the same mood

variations.display: Sī pretium magnum est, nōn solvō.
variations.cue: If the price is high, I am not paying.
variations.changed: both halves plain, which is the open condition

variations.display: Sī mercēs magna sit, nōn solvam.
variations.cue: If the rent were high, I should not pay.
variations.changed: a feminine noun, so two words move

mistake.display: Sī pretium magnum est, nōn solvam.
mistake.why: one half plain and one in the mood, which is M4's error five modules later. It is at its most tempting here because -am can be a future: the sentence reads as a real condition with a promise after it, and it is neither one thing nor the other.

sentences.usage: Said setting a limit before you look.
sentences.mnemonic: sī plus sit makes -am a mood.

sentences.display: Quantī cōnstat? Melius est nōn emere.
sentences.cue: How much is it? It is better not to buy.
sentences.literal: at-how-much it-stands better it-is not to-buy

words.note: 'At how much?' — a GENITIVE of price, which L1-M8 taught as a whole phrase and could not explain. Now it can: quantī cōnstat is 'at how much does it stand?'
'It costs', literally 'it stands together'. L1-M8's whole phrase, now with a reason.
'Better' — L2-M9's melior in the neuter, doing an adverb's job. M7's frame.
The verb 'to be' in the shapes this level writes: sum 'I am', es 'you are', est 'he/she/it is', sunt 'they are'.
'Not', and it denies the infinitive: what is better is not-buying.
'To buy' — emō's infinitive. L1-M8's verb, and its subjunctive emam is the mood M4 opened: another -am that could be a future.

sentences.trap: The module's first phrase and M7's advice frame in two clauses, and neither needed anything new. quantī cōnstat is L1-M8's and melius est nōn emere is M7's — twenty-eight modules of ladder, and the last sentence of this one is built entirely out of it.
sentences.sound: QUAN-tī CŌN-stat? ME-li-us EST nōn E-me-re. Two long vowels in the question and one in the answer.

variations.display: Quantī cōnstat? Melius est nōn solvere.
variations.cue: How much is it? It is better not to pay.
variations.changed: this module's verb instead of L1-M8's

variations.cue: How much is it? I want to buy it.
variations.changed: a decision instead of advice

variations.display: Pretium magnum est; melius est nōn emere.
variations.cue: The price is high; it is better not to buy.
variations.changed: the price stated rather than asked

sentences.usage: Said walking away from a purchase.
sentences.mnemonic: Nothing new in the last sentence, on purpose.
